Donax hanleyanus, a common intertidal bivalve inhabiting sandy beaches along the Atlantic coast of South America, exhibits a suite of life-history traits characteristic of a rapidly growing wedge clam. Field surveys indicate that the maximum shell length attained by this species is approximately 4.4 centimeters [Li = approximately 4.4 centimeters], a size that is comparatively modest within the Donacidae family. Juveniles commence shell growth rapidly after settlement, and detailed growth increment analyses have revealed that the shell length at which individuals first attain reproductive capability is 1.4 centimeters [Lp = 1.4 centimeters]. This early onset of pubertal size, reaching less than a third of the ultimate length, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive investment, a pattern often observed in short-lived bivalves from dynamic sedimentary habitats where adult mortality from wave action and predation is unpredictable and frequently high.

Investigations into the early developmental stages of Donax hanleyanus have provided precise data on the mass of newly released offspring. Following external fertilisation, the resulting embryonated eggs develop into free-swimming veliger larvae that rely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to planktotrophic feeding. The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of a newly hatched veliger, has been estimated at 0.00000097 grams [Wwb = 0.00000097 grams]. This extraordinarily low birth mass, derived from an egg diameter of approximately 123 micrometers, reflects the minute energetic capital invested per offspring and underscores the species' reliance on high fecundity as a primary reproductive strategy. By comparison, the ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult is considerably larger, reaching 3.7 grams [Wwi = 3.7 grams], a value that represents a substantial increase of over six orders of magnitude from the birth stage and implies a prolonged period of rapid somatic growth.

Reproductive output in Donax hanleyanus has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions that approximate its natural habitat. At a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], females demonstrate a remarkably high annual fecundity, producing approximately 575 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 575 eggs per day], which reflects the maximum reproductive rate recorded for the species under these conditions. This elevated daily egg production is sustained over the spawning season, and when integrated across an entire year, the total annual fecundity reaches several hundred thousand eggs per female. Such a strategy of copious egg production is characteristic of broadcast-spawning bivalves that face high larval mortality during the planktonic phase, where the probability of successful settlement and recruitment is extremely low despite the massive numerical output of gametes released into the water column.

Longevity records for Donax hanleyanus, gathered from mark-recapture studies and growth ring analyses, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5.2 years [am = approximately 5.2 years] when individuals are maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is consistent with the species' rapid growth trajectory and early reproductive maturation, as individuals channel a significant proportion of their acquired energy into gamete production rather than prolonged somatic maintenance. The onset of senescence becomes apparent after the third year, as growth rates decelerate markedly and shell condition deteriorates, leading to increased vulnerability to both physical disturbance and predation from crustaceans and demersal fishes that forage within the swash zone of exposed sandy beaches along its distributional range.

Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that Donax hanleyanus occupies an intermediate position within the genus in terms of both body size and life-history pace. While its ultimate shell length of 4.4 centimeters [Li = 4.4 centimeters] is smaller than that of the larger Donax trunculus, which can exceed 4.7 centimeters, the asymptotic wet mass of 3.7 grams [Wwi = 3.7 grams] is size-corrected relative to that species and suggests a similar overall body density. The shell length at puberty of 1.4 centimeters [Lp = 1.4 centimeters] implies that reproductive maturation occurs at a proportionally smaller size compared to some other Donax species, a trait that may confer a demographic advantage in frequently disturbed intertidal zones where the probability of surviving to a larger size is low. This suite of traits, including a short lifespan and high fecundity, positions Donax hanleyanus as an opportunistic species well adapted to the harsh and variable conditions of high-energy sandy beaches.
